Explore / How are borrower reach, savers/depositors, nominal portfolio and provider structure changing in microfinance?

Finance: borrower, saver and balance figures measure different things

Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active microfinance borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020; a 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023, for a set of providers that has not yet been verified. Saver, portfolio and bank balance-sheet figures use different definitions, provider coverage and valuation bases, so this resource keeps them separate and does not read them as one trend or as deeper inclusion.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
Reading rule

Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment.

What the finance evidence does not establish

Savers or depositors are not necessarily unique people. Nominal portfolio growth is not real credit deepening. A listed microfinance bank is not proof of operation or outreach. A same-year restatement is not an economic boom. Historical or secondary borrower figures are not a current national inclusion rate, and these separate data points do not establish improved borrower outcomes or causality.

What remains unresolved

This resource still lacks a fully harmonized current institution-level series that reconciles provider coverage, borrower and saver definitions, deduplication, currency and valuation basis, nominal versus real values, and comparable reporting periods. The underlying 2023 SFD/SMED primary source behind several secondary figures has been identified but is not yet available for direct verification. Microfinance portfolio figures are also not expressed here as a share of bank credit: twelve microfinance banks appear on the same CBY-Aden bank list, so the two stocks may overlap, and they differ in valuation basis, date and institutional coverage.

01
Analysis

Microfinance history is informative, but not a continuous annual series

The historical record contains exact quarterly and year-end observations, pointer-only years and years with no usable observation. In 2015, primary SFD evidence shows active borrowers declining from 124,917 at end-March to 106,825 at end-September and 93,118 at end-December, alongside a declining reported portfolio. This resource keeps those observed points and gaps as they are; it does not interpolate the missing months or estimate a causal conflict effect.

02
Analysis

Borrowers, savers and nominal portfolio do not form one harmonized trend

Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023; the set of providers it covers has not yet been verified. That paper also reports what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” and a nominal portfolio of about YER 44 billion in 2023. The verified 2020 anchors are 1.611 million savers/depositors and YER 33.379 billion; “active savers” and “savers/depositors” have not been shown to be the same measure. Both portfolio figures are nominal rials. Between December 2020 and December 2023 the average market rate published by the Central Bank in Aden moved from 792.69 to 1,529.4 rials per US dollar, and the evidence base does not record which rial valuation, across Yemen's divided monetary areas, the portfolio figures use. No real or US-dollar change can be derived from the two figures. With the 2023 primary source document, provider coverage, saver definition and period bridge also unresolved, these values are separate data points, not a trend.

A view that changes understanding

Borrowers, savers and loan portfolio: separate dated anchors, not one series

Analytical text alternative
  1. Analytical question: What does the available microfinance evidence show about borrowers, savers and portfolio size over time?
  2. What the evidence shows: Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified tables record 93,118 active borrowers and 509,590 savers at end-2015, and 88,445 borrowers and 1.611 million savers/depositors at end-2020. The loan portfolio is YER 6.741 billion at end-2015 in the provider table, while the source narrative gives a figure near YER 9 billion, and YER 33.379 billion at end-2020. A 2024 policy paper by the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, citing SFD/SMED loan-portfolio data, reports 78,686 borrowers, what it calls 3.3 million “active savers” and a nominal portfolio of about YER 44 billion for end-2023; the set of providers it covers has not been verified. “Active savers” and “savers/depositors” have not been shown to be the same measure, and the evidence base does not record which rial valuation, across Yemen’s divided monetary areas, the portfolio figures use. The figures are therefore separate dated anchors: they do not show a trend or a divergence, and they do not establish unique people, real credit deepening or a US-dollar change.
  3. Scope and time: end-2015, end-2020 and end-2023 (secondary source), plus a contextual finding through 2021 · Microfinance institutions and banks as covered by each source (providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development for 2015 and 2020); the set of providers covered in 2023 and the deduplication of savers are unresolved
  4. What not to conclude: The anchors are not a harmonized trend or evidence of divergence. They do not show growth in unique people, real credit deepening, broader inclusion, better borrower outcomes or a causal effect of the conflict.
03
Analysis

Who provides microfinance: what the lists and panels show

Of the 26 banks on the list of licensed banks issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), as checked on 7 September 2026, 12 are identified by the source label as microfinance banks; appearing on the list establishes listing, not operation or outreach. Historical microfinance figures come from provider reporting panels whose membership changes — the 2014 panel, for example, covers nine providers — so provider counts and totals from different periods are not one continuous series.

04
Evidence

A published balance-sheet jump can partly be a valuation change

The same 2022 consolidated banking positions are published at materially higher levels from the 2023 annual-report vintage onward, alongside a documented January-2023 shift to market-exchange-rate valuation of foreign-currency positions. The published difference does not by itself establish growth in assets, deposits or credit because the restatement changes the comparison base.

05
System context

Finance sits between funding, providers and real economic use

Institutional finance connects funding and liquidity to providers, credit products, firms and households. But each link has a different measure: capital available to an institution is not credit disbursed; portfolio is not borrowers; borrowers are not unique households; and larger loans are not necessarily wider outreach. This resource links Finance to Firms, Providers and external flows while preserving those boundaries.

More evidence and contextAdditional controlled detail from this route, preserved with its original boundaries.
System context

Balance-sheet capacity is visible; a complete current financial-soundness diagnosis is not

The compiled monetary series provide balance-sheet context on bank deposits, credit to the private sector, bank reserves, capital and reserves, loans and advances, and foreign-currency deposits across their available reporting periods. These measures help describe intermediation capacity and structure, but they are not a complete current financial-soundness assessment: solvency, asset quality or current system-wide soundness cannot be inferred from balance-sheet aggregates alone. The current evidence base does not yet contain a harmonized, publication-ready set of non-performing-loan, capital-adequacy and liquidity ratios with common definitions and vintages.

Analysis

External support also has financial states that cannot be added indiscriminately

A pledge, commitment, signed agreement, deposit, amount made available, budget disbursement, FX-auction use, in-kind support and project cost are different states. They may describe the same support pathway at different stages or overlapping components. This resource therefore does not manufacture a cumulative finance total by adding unlike states.

System context

The financial system changed through shocks, constraints and policy responses — not one continuous trend

The documented chronology traces several distinct breaks: reserve and import-finance pressure by 2015–16; the 2016 central-bank split; rapid growth of currency outside banks by 2017; Saudi reserve support in 2018 and 2023; the 2019 split-cash/payment episode; the oil-export shock after 2022; FX auctions and external support in 2023–24; banking-liquidity stress and administrative FX/import measures in 2025; and later payment-infrastructure investment. Each event keeps its territorial and institutional scope; where money is involved, agreement, deposit, availability, disbursement and downstream use are kept apart and never added together; and same-year remittance revisions are kept separate from economic change. These events help explain the environment in which finance operates, but their sequence does not prove that any one event caused a financial-inclusion outcome.

System context

An evidence-based chronology of the financial system

The dated events below help explain the conditions under which finance operates: funding and liquidity pressures, exchange-rate conditions, intermediation and payment infrastructure. Each event opens a record with its source and limitations. The chronology is context, not a causal model of financial inclusion.

Demand-side evidence

Holding a product and owning an account are related — not interchangeable

Product-holding and mobile-access figures attributed to the OECD's 2026 financial-sector review have not yet been verified against the review's own text, and they are not shown here. Any such measures would in any case use questions and constructs different from the Global Findex account-ownership measure and would remain separate evidence rather than a harmonised series. Product holding, account ownership, device access and financial-service use must not be averaged or treated as interchangeable.

Dated events in Yemen's financial system

Each event keeps its date, its source and what it does not establish. The order of events does not show that one caused another.

  1. 2014–2015

    The conflict that escalated from late 2014 disrupted output, public finance, external inflows and monetary conditions; by late 2015 official foreign reserves had fallen below US$2 billion, about two months of imports.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: This conditions banks, import finance, cash demand and service continuity.

    Does not establish: It does not quantify population financial inclusion in 2015 or attribute later inclusion outcomes to one shock.

    Sources: Yemen's Economic Outlook, Spring 2016 · Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)

  2. February 2016

    With reserves under pressure, the Central Bank of Yemen stopped supporting imports at the official exchange rate except for wheat and rice.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Import-finance constraints affect liquidity, prices, firms and trade-settlement channels, but are not themselves an inclusion measure.

    Does not establish: It does not show which households or firms lost financial-service access.

    Sources: Yemen's Economic Outlook, Spring 2016

  3. September 2016

    A 2016 decision relocated the Central Bank of Yemen from Sana'a to Aden, leaving two central-bank authorities operating under the divided political and territorial order.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Provider status, payment interoperability, cash conditions and formal financial access can diverge by territory.

    Does not establish: Institutional fragmentation does not by itself prove that a specific provider or service stopped operating in a specific location.

    Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): appraisal document (project approved 17 June 2025)

  4. 2017–2018

    World Bank monitoring estimated currency outside banks rose from YER810.9 billion in 2014 to YER1,673 billion by end-2017, alongside large issuance of new banknotes and rapid expected money-supply growth in 2018.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: It provides context for cash dependence and pressure on formal intermediation.

    Does not establish: Currency outside banks is not equal to household cash holdings, exclusion, or the number of unbanked people.

    Sources: Yemen Economic Monitoring Brief, Fall 2018

  5. January–March 2018

    Saudi Arabia directed and then signed an agreement to deliver a US$2 billion deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen, intended to support the financial/economic position and the riyal.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Stabilization and import-finance support can affect firms, prices and banking liquidity indirectly.

    Does not establish: The signed amount is not identical to later FX sales and is not an inclusion outcome.

    Sources: Saudi directive and agreement on a US$2 billion deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (January–March 2018)

  6. December 2019

    Tighter enforcement in Sana'a of the ban on newer rial banknotes contributed to a payments crisis and widened dual exchange rates between old and new notes across the divided monetary areas.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: A nominally available transfer or payment channel may have different usability and cost by territory.

    Does not establish: It does not quantify unique users switching to digital finance or prove durable digital adoption.

    Sources: Yemen Monthly Economic Update, December 2019

  7. Early 2020

    World Bank monitoring reported that the bulk of the 2018 Saudi US$2 billion deposit had been exhausted by end-January 2020 and highlighted multiple exchange-rate regimes and remittance risks from the COVID-19 shock.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Remittances matter as both household flows and part of broader FX/payment conditions.

    Does not establish: A stated risk to remittances is not an observed decline unless separately measured.

    Sources: Yemen's Economic Update, April 2020

  8. October 2022–January 2023

    Attacks on oil export facilities in October 2022 were followed by the suspension of oil exports from January 2023, sharply reducing a major source of government and foreign-exchange revenue in areas under the internationally recognized government.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Bank liquidity, FX availability, firm finance and payment conditions need to be read against this external-revenue break.

    Does not establish: The oil-export shock does not itself quantify access to financial services or household adoption.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)

  9. 21 February 2023

    Saudi Arabia signed a US$1 billion deposit agreement with the Central Bank of Yemen and stated that the amount was fully deposited in the bank's account.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: The link to inclusion is indirect through macro stability, banking and import-finance conditions.

    Does not establish: The US$0.775 billion later made available and the downstream FX-auction use are part of the same US$1 billion, not additional support.

    Sources: Agreement on a US$1 billion Saudi deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (21 February 2023)

  10. 2023–2024

    The IMF reports US$1.2 billion in Saudi budget support over 2023–24 and a US$1 billion deposit at the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), of which US$0.775 billion had been made available; CBY-Aden auctioned US$1.05 billion for import financing during 2023–24.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: These flows condition formal banking and firm activity but are not direct inclusion outcomes.

    Does not establish: The US$1.05 billion of FX auctions is downstream use of support already counted, not a separate donor inflow.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80) · Agreement on a US$1 billion Saudi deposit to the Central Bank of Yemen (21 February 2023)

  11. 2022–2024

    In the IMF’s macroeconomic framework for areas under the internationally recognized government, the current-account deficit improved from about 40.5% of GDP in 2022 to an average of about 14.5% in 2023–24, reflecting import compression, strong remittances and bilateral grants despite the halt in oil exports.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Remittances, imports and FX conditions interact, but the aggregate balance does not reveal who used formal services.

    Does not establish: The deficit improvement is not proof of stronger household welfare, financial inclusion or productive investment.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)

  12. March–June 2024

    A new 100-rial coin in Sana'a in March 2024 was followed by an April CBY-Aden directive for banks headquartered in Sana'a to relocate to Aden and further June measures affecting unlicensed entities, wallets, payment services and remittance networks.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: The same provider name can carry different regulatory and operational meanings by territory.

    Does not establish: A directive or prohibition does not prove actual compliance, closure, relocation or user access at every location.

    Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): appraisal document (project approved 17 June 2025)

  13. By 30 May 2024

    World Bank/G2Px reported that Yemen's Unconditional Cash Transfer programme had piloted digital payments in eight districts, benefiting 45,460 recipients, with the pilot emphasizing payments into fully functional accounts and recipient choice.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: This is direct Yemen evidence that a social transfer can create formal account exposure. Durable inclusion still requires follow-up on activation, repeat transactions, merchant use, saving, cash-out, cost and user experience.

    Does not establish: The 45,460 recipients are not evidence of 45,460 persistent active users, a national inclusion rate, or sustained post-transfer digital use.

    Sources: Digitalizing Government-to-Person (G2P) Payments in Yemen: unconditional cash transfer (UCT) pilot (2024)

  14. 2024 value revised across CBY annual-report vintages

    The 2024 annual report of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) gives remittances for 2024 of USD 6,245 million; its 2025 annual report restates the same year at USD 3,422.16 million, a downward revision of about 45.2%.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Remittance trend analysis must expose vintage and method changes before drawing behavioral conclusions.

    Does not establish: A revised 2024 level is not evidence that remittances collapsed by 45.2% during 2024.

    Sources: Annual Report 2024 · Annual Report 2025

  15. 2022–April 2025

    In the IMF's banking data for areas under the internationally recognized government, the liquid-assets to short-term-liabilities ratio fell from 148 in 2022 to 69 in April 2025, while the capital-to-assets ratio fell from about 5 to about 2.5.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Provider resilience and usable service capacity are system conditions for inclusion.

    Does not establish: Prudential ratios do not show how many unique people gained or lost access.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)

  16. July 2025 onward

    The government established the National Committee for the Regulation and Financing of Imports to prioritize FX for essential imports, improve import transparency and channel FX through the formal banking sector.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: This may change incentives and flows through banks and exchangers, which should be measured.

    Does not establish: Creation of the committee does not prove improved access, lower costs or successful formalization.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)

  17. Mid-July–early August 2025

    The IMF reports the rial, in markets in areas under the internationally recognized government, strengthening from about YER2,900 to about YER1,600 per US dollar from mid-July to early August 2025 after a package of FX and market measures.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Exchange-rate conditions affect prices, remittance conversion, firm costs and channel incentives.

    Does not establish: The appreciation does not by itself prove durable macro stability or improved financial inclusion.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)

  18. September 2025

    The IMF reports operational foreign-exchange reserves of about US$350 million in September 2025, covering roughly one month of imports.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Reserve scarcity conditions import finance, bank liquidity and prices.

    Does not establish: Import-cover reserves do not measure household financial resilience or account use.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: 2025 Article IV Consultation — Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/80)

  19. 17 June 2025–2030 project period

    The World Bank approved a US$20 million IDA grant for the Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (P180708) on 17 June 2025. The project is active, implemented by UNDP, closes on 30 June 2030, and the latest disclosed ISR identified in this review is sequence 2 dated 8 April 2026.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: The project can create payment-system capacity and targeted access/usage mechanisms, while population adoption and inclusion effects require later evidence.

    Does not establish: The US$20 million commitment, an implementation report, a system go-live or a 2030 target is not evidence that users have already adopted services or that inclusion outcomes have been achieved.

    Sources: Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP, P180708): project record and results framework (2025–2030) · Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP): implementation overview (2025–2030) · Yemen Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP): Implementation Status and Results Report, sequence 2 (8 April 2026)

  20. 1 March 2026

    The Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen signed an agreement with Yemen's Ministry of Finance to begin depositing SAR1.3 billion in economic support for operating expenses and salaries.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: It can affect public cash flow, salaries, demand and macro conditions.

    Does not establish: The SAR1.3 billion agreement is not shown to be the same flow as IMF-reported USD commitments or disbursements; no source-level crosswalk establishes that. An agreement to deposit is not evidence that a deposit or a disbursement has taken place.

    Sources: Agreement between the Saudi Development and Reconstruction Program for Yemen (SDRPY) and Yemen's Ministry of Finance on SAR1.3 billion in economic support (1 March 2026)

  21. 4 June 2026

    The World Bank Group endorsed a Country Partnership Framework for Yemen for FY2026–FY2030 and approved four new operations totaling US$285 million. The framework focuses on nutrition, electricity, agribusiness, mariculture and fisheries, with women’s participation and private-sector development as cross-cutting enablers.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: This context helps interpret firm finance, payment infrastructure and participation constraints as connected parts of a wider economic system.

    Does not establish: Endorsement of a strategy or approval of operations does not prove improved financial access, service use, jobs, implementation quality or inclusion outcomes.

    Sources: Republic of Yemen: Country Partnership Framework for FY2026–FY2030

  22. 30 June 2026

    The World Bank approved a US$100 million IDA grant for the Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project in Yemen. The project is expected to reach 1.8 million people, support around 55,000 individuals through Village Savings and Loan Associations, and support more than 675,000 people in obtaining national identity cards and birth certificates; these are project design and target states, not achieved results.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Identity documentation and savings-group participation are potentially important enabling steps that should be measured separately from account ownership, active use and service quality.

    Does not establish: Project targets, beneficiary counts, identity-document support and VSLA participation do not establish national prevalence, active bank or wallet use, or persistence after programme support ends.

    Sources: Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project, Yemen (approved 30 June 2026)

  23. 16 July 2026

    IMF staff and the Yemeni authorities reached a staff-level agreement on policies that could underpin a proposed 18-month Staff-Monitored Program. The agreement is subject to IMF Management approval, and the IMF press release on the mission states that it will not result in an Executive Board discussion; priorities include fiscal and monetary management, reserve rebuilding, and financial-sector and electricity reforms.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: Financial-sector reform commitments matter for intermediation, resilience and oversight, while inclusion effects require later evidence on provider behaviour, access, use, cost, quality and protection.

    Does not establish: A staff-level agreement does not establish IMF financing, Executive Board approval, completed reforms, improved bank soundness or improved financial inclusion.

    Sources: Yemen: staff-level agreement on a proposed Staff-Monitored Program (16 July 2026)

  24. Current analytical rule

    The chronology treats remittances, international support, FX auctions, import compression, reserve changes, bank liquidity, regulatory actions and payment infrastructure as related but non-interchangeable kinds of evidence.

    Relevance to financial inclusion: This is the bridge from macro-financial chronology to inclusion decisions: capacity, access, use, quality and outcomes remain separate states.

    Does not establish: Chronological proximity never substitutes for causal identification.

Evidence Readings on this question

Evidence Reading

When a balance sheet jumps without the economy necessarily moving

Published banking stocks for the same reference period shift materially across vintages alongside a documented valuation change. A change in measurement basis can account for part of the published shift and needs to be separated from economic movement before intermediation or scale is interpreted.

Evidence Reading

Borrower counts, savers and nominal portfolio can move differently

Borrower, saver and portfolio figures cannot yet be read as one story. Among providers reporting to the Social Fund for Development (SFD), verified primary tables record 93,118 active borrowers at end-2015 and 88,445 at end-2020, and a 2024 secondary source citing SFD/SMED data reports 78,686 for end-2023 for a set of providers not yet verified; with provider coverage and the period bridge unresolved, even these are separate data points rather than a trend. The saver and portfolio figures use different definitions and are nominal rials whose valuation across Yemen’s divided monetary areas is not recorded, so they cannot show whether saving or credit deepened. The evidence supports separate data points, not a story of ‘growth’, ‘deepening’ or ‘divergence’.

What measurement would change the decision?

A current MSME finance demand/use baseline

A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome.

This evidence would show the finance journey from need and application through approval or rejection, terms, use and repayment pressure, while SMEPS remains a separate programme-evidence layer.
Open this measurement priority

Credit-infrastructure reach and actual use

Administrative data from credit-information and collateral infrastructure and participating institutions on coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation and borrower type.

This evidence would show whether credit infrastructure enters actual lending decisions, for which lenders and borrower groups.
